title: The Dead Salmons of AI Interpretability
claim: Standard analyses report apparent structure and predictive signal even in randomly initialized models, revealing false discoveries from uncorrected inference.
layout: 2 panels: heatmap on top, cartoon plus line plot below; humorous MRI illustration
description: The figure has two panels. Panel A is a large heatmap titled 'PCA components (correlation with label)' with the orange subtitle 'colored means p < 0.05'. The y-axis is layers and the x-axis is principal components. Most cells are pale gray. Scattered orange and yellow cells, clustered near the middle columns, mark nominally significant correlations. Bottom left is a cartoon of a Sesame Street-style character lying in an MRI scanner. A monitor beside it shows a speckled activation map, and the caption below reads 'Randomized'. This is a nod to the dead salmon study. Panel B, bottom right, is a line plot of probe accuracy against layers 0–12. An orange line with a shaded band sits around 0.75–0.8, above a dashed gray 'Random Guessing' line at 0.5. The eye goes first to the heatmap and then to the cartoon.
caption: Exhibit of minimal dead salmon artifacts. We extract token representations from a randomly initialized BERT for 300 IMDb sentences and average over sequence length. (A) Each cell is a (layer, principal component) pair of the mean-pooled activations; coloured cells are those whose Pearson correlation with the binary sentiment label has a two-sided p < 0.05. No correction for multiple comparisons is applied, on purpose: the panel shows what an uncorrected pipeline returns, as in the original study, and these individually weak correlations are not expected to survive a Bonferroni or Benjamini–Hochberg correction [Benjamini and Hochberg, 1995]. (B) A simple probe trained on layer representations achieves nontrivial cross-validated accuracy.
abstract: In a striking neuroscience study, the authors placed a dead salmon in an MRI scanner and showed it images of humans in social situations. Astonishingly, standard analyses of the time reported brain regions predictive of social emotions. The explanation, of course, was not supernatural cognition but a cautionary tale about misapplied statistical inference. In AI interpretability, reports of similar "dead salmon" artifacts abound: feature attribution, probing, sparse auto-encoding, and even causal analyses can produce plausible-looking explanations for randomly initialized neural networks. Upon inspection of this phenomenon our position is to argue for a pragmatic statistical-causal reframing: explanations of computational systems should be treated as parameters of a (statistical) model, inferred from computational traces. This perspective goes beyond simply measuring statistical variability of explanations due to finite sampling of input data; interpretability methods become statistical estimators, and findings should be tested against explicit and meaningful alternative computational hypotheses, with uncertainty quantified with respect to the postulated statistical model. It also highlights important theoretical issues, such as the identifiability of common interpretability queries, which we argue is critical to understand the field's susceptibility to false discoveries, poor generalizability, and high variance.
